prize_parts.citation: For the invention of the optical lattice clock, in which neutral atoms are trapped at the magic wavelength, and its development to fractional uncertainties near 1e-18

statement.case_for: My preferred configuration is unchanged: a single prize for the optical lattice clock to Katori and Ye. Having read the full exchange, I think the case is stronger than in round 1 because the objections raised against it concern category and scope, not the science. Nobody disputes that the magic-wavelength idea is original, that it was realised in several independent laboratories, or that 1e-18 uncertainties have been reproduced and intercompared. The physics also feeds back into fundamental questions: the clock is only meaningful at this level because polarisabilities, blackbody shifts and higher-order light shifts are controlled in atoms such as strontium and ytterbium, and the same clocks now constrain drifts of constants, resolve gravitational redshift across millimetre-scale samples and are used in dark-matter searches. That is why I do not accept a hard line between discovery and instrument here. The committee can state a scope that separates this from earlier prizes: the 2005 prize concerned the optical frequency comb and comb-based precision spectroscopy, the 2012 prize concerned control of individual trapped quantum systems including single-ion clocks, and the 2026 citation would concern interrogating many neutral atoms at once in an engineered light-shift-free lattice, which is a different physical route to accuracy and stability. In response to Pearce's question, I would describe Ye's role as a distinct and decisive contribution to realising the concept at record performance rather than a separate invention: ultrastable cavity-stabilised lasers, systematic control and many-body (spin-squeezing and high-density) operation took the strontium clock from the first demonstrations to the 1e-18 regime. Katori supplied the concept and the first demonstrations, and the two roles are linked rather than parallel.
statement.case_against: The credit boundary remains the strongest reservation. Lemonde and the SYRTE group, Takamoto, Ludlow, Hinkley, Sterr and the PTB group, and Gill and the ion-clock community all contributed to early lattice demonstrations and to the stability record, and two names cannot capture that. A second reservation is that the largest consequences, such as a redefinition of the second, relativistic geodesy as routine practice and constant-drift searches, are still prospective, so critics can say the prize rewards a capability whose scientific payoff is still ahead. I take that seriously, but I do not find it decisive, since the redefinition does not have to occur first and the capability has already produced measurements no earlier standard could make. I also recognise that if the committee holds firmly to a discovery-of-a-new-phenomenon criterion, B022 is the stronger fit for that criterion even though it is less mature.

responses.point: Pearce asked whether Ye's role is better described as an accuracy and many-body programme or as a distinct invention, because that determines the citation wording, and proposed writing the citation around the lattice clock and its accuracy rather than spectroscopy in general.
responses.response: I would call it the accuracy and many-body programme, and I would not present it as a separate invention. The citation should therefore name the lattice clock as the invention and the 1e-18 regime as its development, which is how I have worded mine. I agree entirely with his point about avoiding spectroscopy in general, since that would reopen the 2005 comb prize. I would add that Ye's contribution is not only incremental accuracy: the cavity-stabilised laser and the control of density-dependent shifts changed what could be measured, which justifies naming him beside Katori. I also agree with his reasoning for keeping B037 apart from this prize.

responses.point: Danielsson rejects dropping Bistritzer from B022, arguing that the 2011 continuum-model paper is a two-author paper and that the first author of the decisive theory cannot be left out when a three-person prize has room.
responses.response: He is right on the credit, and I change my view on that point. The 2011 prediction is a two-author paper, and a three-person limit leaves room, so if B022 were advanced I would now name MacDonald, Jarillo-Herrero and Bistritzer. I do not think this changes the ranking between B022 and B025: he is the only member who prefers B022, and the experimental credit beyond Jarillo-Herrero, namely Cao, Fatemi and the Dean, Young and Kim groups, remains unresolved. On discovery versus capability, I agree that B022 delivered a surprising phenomenon quickly. I still put the clock first because its interpretation is stable and quantitatively confirmed, whereas the pairing mechanism and twist-angle disorder remain open, and his own wording would require a citation that avoids claiming a mechanism.

responses.point: Olsson proposes that the 1e-18 uncertainty figures and the chronology of the first lattice clocks be verified against primary intercomparisons before the citation is fixed, and that the citation name the concept and its realisation without claiming the whole field.
responses.response: I agree on both. I also relied on recalled values in round 1 and have not checked them against the primary papers here. I would state the citation as near 1e-18 and not as a specific figure, and I would have the committee secretariat verify the chronology of the first strontium lattice demonstrations (Katori's proposal, the first RIKEN and Tokyo results, and the near-simultaneous JILA, SYRTE and PTB work) so that the credit statement is correct. Concerning her recusal question, I see no reason why her Japanese institutional connections require her to stand back, since nothing documents a collaboration with Katori, but I would leave that to the committee. I also thank her for explaining why she does not press B008.

responses.point: Kroll argues that discovery versus instrument should not be a hard line, citing the Charpak and Hall-Haensch precedents, and that the nuclear-clock work is not mature enough to compete, so Ye is credited once and for the lattice clock.
responses.response: I agree with the precedent argument and with treating the thorium-229 work as not yet mature, so Ye is credited once. I qualify one point: the Hall-Haensch precedent is also the reason the committee must write a scope sentence, since it is the nearest earlier prize in the lineage. His disclosure of a stay in Hall's laboratory is, in my view, field proximity and not a conflict, and it is similar to my own knowledge of the community. I also note that he and I are the two who placed B025 first at the opening, so we should be careful not to treat our shared view as an independent confirmation of the others.

uncertainties: The division of credit between Katori's concept, Ye's performance programme and the contributions of Lemonde, Takamoto, Ludlow, Hinkley, Sterr and Gill, which two names cannot fully represent.

Whether the committee accepts that a measurement capability with partly prospective consequences meets the criterion of discovery or invention, and whether the scope statement separates it convincingly from the 2005 and 2012 prizes.
The exact 1e-18 figures and the chronology of the first lattice clocks, which I am recalling and which should be checked against primary comparisons.
Whether B022 would be better placed in a later cycle once the pairing mechanism is clearer.
statement.conflict_note: No documented tie to Katori or Ye. My documented collaborators (the Gothenburg group, L'Huillier, the Lund attosecond group, Keller's group at ETH, Schuch, Dahlstrom, Argenti and Indelicato) do not include either of them. As an atomic theorist I work in the same community and know the field, and I have worked on atomic structure related to highly charged ions and precision spectroscopy, so I record that as field proximity and not as a conflict. I see no reason to recuse myself on B025, B022 or B036, and I would defer to the committee on the disclosures made by Olsson and Kroll.
